title: Model curation playbook & runtime-fit walkthrough - Blue Mesa
summary: AE + SE walkthrough of the model catalog, curated playbooks for open models, benchmark comparators and runtime compatibility guidance. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for latency-sensitive recommender inference; main asks: end-to-end cost estimates, SOC2 + SSO, and a short pilot on P40/RTX configs.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-08-05 16:00 PT | Duration ~58m | Attendees: Riley (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marcus (Redwood CSM), Jordan (CTO Blue Mesa), Samantha (ML Eng), Evan (Platform)

[00:00] Riley: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call? just so we know who we have on the line.
[00:08] Jordan: Jordan here, CTO, Blue Mesa. We have Samantha and Evan with me.
[00:12] Samantha: hi
[00:14] Evan: yep, Evan here.
[00:16] Riley: Great. I'm Riley, AE, and Priya will run through the catalog and runtime fit shortly. Marcus is on to help with compliance questions.
[00:25] Priya: cool, um, I'll share my screen — I'm going to go through the model curation playbook first then demo the catalog filters and the compatibility matrix. There's a short bench slide pack too.
[00:36] Riley: The goal today from our side is to show how you can pick an open model, compare perf vs cost, and choose a runtime profile for either hosted or dedicated. Jordan, you mentioned low-latency recommender in the invite, is that still the primary use-case?
[00:49] Jordan: yes, p50 < 100ms ideally for 512 tokens; throughput is moderate — maybe 50 rps at peak. We're also sensitive to per-token cost because the service is internal and high-volume.
[01:02] Priya: okay good, that helps. So first slide: our curated model playbooks — these are opinionated sets of models tuned to workloads. For recommenders we usually point customers at smaller decoder-only models and sparse attention variants if you have longer context. For short context, we show quantized 4-bit variants to reduce cost.
[01:24] Samantha: quick question — how accurate are the cost numbers in the catalog? we've seen big delta between vendor benchmarks and real workload.
[01:31] Priya: yeah that’s expected. Catalog numbers are derived from microbenchmarks on representative sequences and typical batch sizes. We include a margin and we always recommend a 24–72 hour pilot with your data to finalize. I can also export a custom spreadsheet that plugs in your distribution.
[01:45] Riley: we can run the pilot on hosted or on dedicated GPUs; for Blue Mesa I'd suggest dedicated P40/RTX pool depending on availability. Evan, any constraints on your infra or VPC needs?
[01:58] Evan: we want VPC peering, SAML SSO, and KMS for key management. Also, we have an internal procurement requirement for SOC2 evidence.
[02:08] Marcus: we have a SOC2 summary and SSO integration guide — I'll share links after. KMS integration exists for both Private and Dedicated deployments.
[02:16] Jordan: good. Also, curious about fallback routing — if the dedicated pool is busy, can we fall back to a cheaper hosted variant automatically?
[02:24] Priya: yes, routing policies can be set by cost vs latency SLO. You can have a primary dedicated variant (pinned model/quant) and fallback to a hosted cooler model — the system will also do automatic format compatibility checking and kv cache warming if models share tokenizer.
[02:38] Samantha: you said "kv cash" earlier in another call — can you clarify how state is handled across fallbacks?
[02:43] Priya: sure — sorry bad transcript, it's KV cache — key-value cache of attention for autoregressive decoding. When we route to a different model variant, if the vocab/tokenizer matches we can rehydrate partial KV; if not, we warm with prefix caching or re-request the initial tokens. There is some overhead when models aren't token-compatible.
[02:58] Riley: demo time — Priya, walk through the catalog UI please.
[03:05] Priya: sharing now. This is the model catalog. Left filters: architecture, quantization, seq length, throughput profile, HW compat. I can pick 'open' models, then show benchmark columns: p50 latency, tokens/sec, batch1 cost, recommended GPU family.
[03:25] [03:30] Priya: I'm selecting a 7B open model variant — we show two quant variants: 4-bit int4 and fp16. Here the int4 shows 1.8x token/sec and 3x cost reduction in our microbench; fp16 gives lower variance but higher cost.
[03:48] Samantha: are those numbers on A100s or on more commodity GPUs?
[03:52] Priya: these particular rows were run on A100 80GB for tail comparison; we also run on T4/RTX and surface a compatibility matrix — see the "HW compat" column. For Blue Mesa we'll surface RTX and P40 profiles since that was mentioned.
[04:08] Evan: what about memory spikes for long context? Does cache size blow up?
[04:12] Priya: KV cache scales roughly linearly with sequence length * hidden size; we display estimated peak memory per token. We also have automatic KV eviction policies for streams and continuous batching to control footprint.
[04:24] Riley: quick interruption — Jordan, what's your expected max sequence? You said 512 earlier but any headroom to 1024?
[04:30] Jordan: 512 typical, sometimes 768 in certain sessions.
[04:34] Priya: okay then we keep the recommended models for 512–768. Next, compatibility matrix view — it's a heatmap mapping model variant vs hardware type and quantization. Green means low-latency fit; amber is okay at higher batch sizes; red is not recommended.
[04:51] [05:00] Priya: note: some open models that are structurally similar show tokenizer mismatch — we flag that. For those we add a compatibility note: "tokenizer mismatch — warming required".
[05:11] Samantha: how do you handle evals — quality regression after quantizing?
[05:16] Priya: two parts: we run unit evals on standard tasks and also encourage customers to run a small holdout promptset. Redwood Optimize will emit a quality delta and alert on regressions when you enable monitoring. We can set a guardrail to fallback to fp16 if quality delta exceeds threshold.
[05:33] Jordan: any examples of customers using int4 in prod? we're wary of hallucinations increasing.
[05:38] Riley: yes, we have customers in search and recommender doing int4 with guardrails — they keep an eval set and run periodic A/B on responses. Priya can share anonymized bench results.
[05:49] Priya: I'll attach the bench pack — it's a small CSV with latencies and output-similarity measures.
[05:56] Evan: for the pilot, we want to test 3 models: smaller decoder 7B int4, a 13B fp16 trimmed, and a 3B quantized low-latency variant. Can Redwood run the microbench on our sample traces?
[06:10] Priya: absolutely, we can reproduce microbench locally if you provide traces. Recommended: send sample of 500 typical queries with distribution of seq-lens and token counts.
[06:20] Jordan: timeline — procurement wants a vendor evaluation within two weeks. We probably need a 3–5 day pilot run and then a decision.
[06:28] Riley: okay we'll aim for a fast turn. Marcus, make sure compliance artifacts are ready.
[06:33] Marcus: will do.
[06:35] [06:40] Riley: let's hit the deeper parts — batching & latency tradeoffs. Priya?
[06:42] Priya: batching increases throughput but can add p50 variance. Our runtime supports dynamic continuous batching and we can configure cutoff windows (e.g., 5–20ms) to balance p50 vs tokens/sec. For your 100ms target, we recommend a small batching window and preferring lower batch sizes on dedicated GPUs.
[07:03] Samantha: and how about model warm-starting — cold start penalties?
[07:06] Priya: cold starts primarily relate to loading weights and cold KV. With dedicated pools, models are pinned and warm, so cold starts are minimal. Hosted may experience cold starts on scale-up; we have warm pools and prefetch options for critical routes.
[07:19] Jordan: what about hybrid routing — keep top traffic on dedicated and overflow to hosted — are pricing deltas visible per route?
[07:26] Riley: yes, per-route cost breakdown is in Console and Optimize; you can see token counts, compute units used, and egress. We'll also show a simulated monthly cost given your expected QPS.
[07:38] [07:45] Priya: switching to the 'optimize' panel — it recommends config: batching window 8ms, int4 quant, and RTX-6000 pool for your distribution. It also lists expected cost per 1M tokens and latency p50/p95. Note: these are estimates not guarantees.
[07:59] Evan: any known gotchas with our infra? we use heavy autoscaling and have ephemeral nodes.
[08:04] Priya: autoscaling interacts with cache locality; on ephemeral nodes you want shorter cache lifespan or a larger warm pool. For long-running sessions, pinned dedicated is preferable.
[08:16] Samantha: security checklist — can you confirm logs retention and access control?
[08:21] Marcus: yes, we have per-token audit logs, retention policy configurable up to X days (we'll provide exact numbers). RBAC integrates with SAML and we support SCIM for provisioning.
[08:31] Jordan: perfect.
[08:34] Riley: a couple of real-world scenarios — if you need absolute p50 < 50ms then we'd recommend smaller model + dedicated A100-like class or aggressive quant + high clock GPUs. If you can accept p50 ~80–100ms, RTX/commodity cards with int4 are the best cost tradeoff.
[08:52] Samantha: curious about model version pinning and rollbacks.
[08:56] Priya: Console supports pinning a model version per route and automated canary rollouts. If you detect quality drift, you can automatically rollback to the previous stable variant and we keep traffic shadowing for A/B.
[09:09] Evan: are there limits on concurrent KV cache size per customer?
[09:13] Priya: not hard limits; we surface estimated memory and will alert on approaching capacity. For on-prem deployments you can tune eviction and shard KV across nodes.
[09:24] [09:30] Riley: okay I want to recap real quick and confirm next steps — Jordan, you need the pricing + spreadsheet, SOC2 + SSO docs, and a pilot scheduled next week yes?
[09:39] Jordan: correct.
[09:41] Riley: action items: we'll send the custom benchmark sheet, Marcus will send SOC2 summary and SAML guide, Priya will coordinate pilot kickoff and we ask Blue Mesa to send sample traces and confirm the three models list.
[09:54] Jordan: sounds good. Any blockers from Redwood on scheduling?
[09:58] Marcus: none from our side.
[10:01] Samantha: one last question — out of curiosity, do you surface per-token embedding costs differently from generation cost? Our recommender has both.
[10:09] Priya: yes embedding endpoints are billed separately and Optimize treats them as a different workload class; it recommends different quant and hardware because embedding models tend to be MLP/encoder-heavy.
[10:22] Evan: ok that's helpful.
[10:25] Riley: Alright, thanks everyone — we'll follow up with links. End note: deck link (model playbook): https://redwood.example/decks/model-playbook.pdf and bench csv: https://redwood.example/benchmarks/bma-sample.csv
[10:40] Jordan: thanks all.
[10:42] Riley: bye.

Notes on transcript fidelity: occasional mis-terms (KV cache -> KV cash) and compressed punctuation reflect auto-transcription artifacts. The call included product demo, qualification, and explicit next steps for pilot and compliance artifacts.
